# The device driver model, and the GPIO and I2C APIs: the exercise

<!-- Generated by tools/maintainer/build_exercise_readmes.py from the lesson page. Edit the lesson, then run the script. -->

Lesson: [The device driver model, and the GPIO and I2C APIs](https://jouhis.github.io/embedded-course/lessons/0098-the-device-driver-model-and.html). Read it first: the steps below refer to its diagrams and worked examples.

## Try it in Wokwi

The starter configures the button as an input. The MYS-1 node, the interrupt setup, the counter and the sensor read are left as TODO(learner) notes.

1. Open `projects/0098-device-driver-i2c/starter` in VS Code, and press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd> to build.
2. In `boards/rpi_pico.overlay`, add the `mystery` node under `&i2c0` at `0x48`, with the compatible `vnd,mystery-sensor`, as in the snippet above. The binding file `dts/bindings/sensor/vnd,mystery-sensor.yaml` is already in the folder.
3. In `prj.conf`, add `CONFIG_I2C=y`.
4. In `src/main.c`, add the sensor spec with `I2C_DT_SPEC_GET`, check `i2c_is_ready_dt()`, and read WHO_AM_I with `i2c_write_read_dt()`. Print `MYSTERY WHO_AM_I 0x%02x` when the value is 0xA7.
5. Still in `main.c`, call `gpio_pin_interrupt_configure_dt` with `GPIO_INT_EDGE_TO_ACTIVE`, then `gpio_init_callback` and `gpio_add_callback_dt`. Finish the callback with the increment.
6. Build, start the simulator, and read the serial monitor. You'll know it works when `MYSTERY WHO_AM_I 0xa7` appears once near the start, and then `button presses N` appears every two seconds. Press the button (the <kbd>b</kbd> key in the diagram) and check that N rises.

In the Wokwi simulator, Zephyr's I2C driver for the RP2040 gets no answer from the MYS-1 chip: the transfer times out (error -116), even though the same chip and wiring answer the Pico SDK code of lesson 63. So in the simulator this lab prints `MYSTERY no answer, error -116` instead of the WHO_AM_I line; the button count still works. The code is right for a real Pico; test the I2C part on the board.

The chip in the diagram is the MYS-1 Wokwi chip from lesson 63, which is compiled to WebAssembly (`mystery.chip.wasm`) and listed in `wokwi.toml` with `[[chip]]`. Our lint does not check custom chips, so the wiring was checked by hand against the chip's pin list. We have not seen this run pass unattended in the simulator, so treat the expected lines above as the target.

If the bus is "not ready", check `build/zephyr/.config` for `CONFIG_I2C=y`. If the read fails, check the address in `reg`. The count only rises after the interrupt is configured, so check that call first.
